Tariffs are a signature policy of Trump's office

The US is preparing to announce new tariffs on several countries, the BBC understands.

The new import taxes would hit many of America's biggest trading partners, with China, the European Union, Mexico and Japan among the 16 jurisdictions affected.

The move comes after the White House's so-called "Section 301" investigation. It was launched in March after the US Supreme Court ruled that President Donald Trump's Liberation Day tariffs were illegal .

Trump has made tariffs a signature policy of his presidency, arguing that they will help boost American manufacturing and create jobs.

The president sent shockwaves around the world when he unveiled sweeping tariffs on global trading partners in April 2025 shortly after his return to the White House.

While the tariffs were later struck down, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer argued then that overproduction abroad was displacing American manufacturing and deterring investment.

Under the new tariffs, countries will face different import tax rates depending on the deals that they have previously struck with Trump.

The announcement is likely to increase tensions between the US and China, the world's two biggest economies, who remain locked in a trade dispute.

Despite last week's meeting between Trump and President Xi Jinping, the two sides have yet to fully resolve their difference with an interim agreement set to expire on 10 January.

In the run up to the Shenzhen summit the US accused China of not fully living up the terms of what it agreed in South Korea in October 2025.

Washington said Beijing was falling short on its commitments, "particularly as they relate to agricultural purchases, rare earths, and other critical minerals".

However earlier on Tuesday China extended the suspension of a ban on exports critical minerals including gallium, germanium, antimony until 27 January. The ban would otherwise have come into force on Friday.

The Trump administration's tariff policy has been criticised for putting up prices for American consumers and damaging the global economy.

Trump's so-called Liberation Day tariffs were struck down by the Supreme Court earlier this year

MN202611_1p2umwlnjdf.t:
Selena Buse, 16, reverses her Citroën Ami out of a parking space and heads off past the school playground. Heads turn. The Ami looks pretty remarkable. Futurist or like-a-toaster depending on your point of view. But it's changed her life.

"I got it because I really needed it to get to school. And I use it to visit friends on the weekends. It's indispensable in rural areas like where I live," she says.

In France, you can drive a car like this from the age of 14 with a road safety certificate and eight hours training. In Italy too.

In Germany and Spain it's 15, in the UK 16. Because they are classed as motorised quadri-cycles. Four-wheel mopeds in other words.

Registrations have risen from about 13,000 in 2019 to around 25,000 last year in France.

In Europe, sales have gone from 30,000 to 60,000 in the past five years. And the Ami, launched in 2020, has really changed the image, with teenagers who now account for a quarter of all mini-car sales.

In Selena's very small Citroën, we are soon rolling along at the top speed of 45km/h (28mph). For other road users, no-licence cars like this can seem like mobile traffic calming.

"When I'm on faster roads and there's a lot of traffic the cars behind me sometimes honk their horns but I can't go any quicker!" Selena says.

Daniel Laprès says the Aixam car was "the exact solution to our problem"

Another local Daniel Laprès, who drives a micro-car made by French firm and market-leader Aixam, tells me he actually pulls over to let the cars behind pass.

He and his wife moved from Paris to this country village two years ago. Of Canadian nationality, he didn't swap his foreign licence for a French one in time and lost the right to drive. That didn't matter much when he was in Paris. Like many Parisians he didn't need a car. He used public transport. But that's not possible here.

"We tried living off of taxis and it was in the end a disaster. Then we heard about how you could drive without having to have a licence, and it was the exact solution to our problem. Cheap, inexpensive to operate, basically no administrative formalities, you get insurance."

However, Laprès feels less safe in his small car. "They're little more than tin cans on wheels, right? I mean, you're not going to be driving fast, but someone else could be."

These cars are forbidden on motorways. But even on medium-fast roads, being considerably slower than the average vehicle can be a problem.

"You go on national highways at your risk and peril. I did it once and I will never, ever do it again. On those roads (speed limit 110km/h), everybody is passing you, including the biggest trucks. And they come at you very fast from the rear, so it's scary," Laprès says.

Daniel is 77 so fits in with the long-established market for these cars: older people living in the countryside.

Traditionally the market also included quite a few people who'd lost their licences, often because of drink-driving offenses. But the launch of the electric Citroën Ami in 2020 changed the customer profile and the product.

"The launch of the Ami was the beginning of the transformation of the sector, with more and more electric models coming on to the market. In 2026, more than 67% of new licence-free cars are electric," says Marie-Laure Nivot, market analyst at AAA Data.

The launch of the Citroën Ami in 2020 "transformed the sector" analysts say

This tendency was encouraged by stricter EU regulations on motorised two-wheelers that had been the vehicles of choice for European teenagers until then.

"It proved too costly for manufacturers to apply the new EU rules, so mopeds and small scooters have almost disappeared from the market since 2020 and licence-free cars have taken their place," Marie-Laure Nivot says.

Tiny car sales rose strongly till 2024 although they have flattened since in France with the withdrawal of subsidies for electric models.

Curiously, the arrival in this niche market of a giant competitor in the shape of Stellantis brand Citroën was actually good news for existing French manufacturers like Aixam and Ligier.

"We're specialised in this niche market and we're very good at what we do, but of course, we didn't have the communication strength of a multinational like Stellantis. They helped us to make people understand that it was possible in France to drive this product from 14-years-old, in Germany from 15-years-old. They gave a lot of visibility to our market," says Aixam sales and marketing director Tom Faget.

Aixam has invested €30m (£25m; $33m) in expanding its production capacity in France. And its sales are growing in other European countries, even as the French market slows.

France's Ligier says young people are choosing tiny cars over scooters

Meanwhile, the competition is producing increasingly sophisticated minicars - some costing as much as a small conventional car. At Ligier, marketing director Romain Illegems says the biggest change is in who's buying them.

"We've gone from mobility that was imposed on people to mobility that people choose. Before, these vehicles were something you used because you absolutely needed to get around, because there was no public transport, or because you didn't have a licence.

"Today, teenagers are choosing them instead of scooters or mopeds, because they're safer and offer better protection from the weather. Young people now account for 40% of our customers."

There are limitations, of course. Just two seats, a maximum speed of 45km/h and no motorways. But for Selena, who rents her Ami for €60 a month, plus insurance, it's a small price to pay for independence.

Energy bills are to soar in January, as prices governed by regulator Ofgem's cap rise at the coldest time of the year.

The cap affects millions of people in England, Scotland and Wales, and reflects higher wholesale gas costs which have been pushed up by the US-Israel war with Iran.

It means people on variable tariffs should give an accurate meter reading, ensure they are receiving all the support to which they are entitled, and take care over energy use.

The energy cap fixes the maximum amount which customers on standard variable tariffs can be charged for each unit of gas and electricity used.

It covers more than 20 million households in England, Wales and Scotland and is set by the regulator Ofgem every three months , external .

It affects those paying by direct debit, by standard credit (they pay when they get a bill), or prepayment meters in slightly different ways.

Most of the increase in the energy price cap has, and will be, driven by higher gas prices.

The government's decision to temporarily remove VAT from domestic electricity bills has cut about £45 a year from a typical bill.

Meanwhile, millions of households will receive a £100 automatic payment to help cover winter costs.

The typical annual usage figure applies to the first category: dual-fuel households on a standard variable tariff which pay by direct debit.

But customers' actual bills depend on the amount of energy used and how they pay for it.

The roughly 11 million households on fixed tariffs do not see their prices change until the end of their fixed term.

Ofgem regulates the energy market in England, Scotland and Wales. Northern Ireland has a separate system.

Although the price cap sets the unit prices for gas and electricity, your household's actual bill depends on the overall amount of energy you use, and how you pay for it.

Where you live, the type of property you have, how energy efficient it is, how many people live there, and the weather all make a difference.

The Ofgem cap is illustrated using "typical" household energy use in a year with a single bill for gas and electricity settled by direct debit.

The vast majority of people pay their bill this way to help spread payments across the year.

In July, Ofgem reduced what it believes to be a "typical" level of energy use, because many homes have cut back due to high prices in recent years while energy efficiency has improved.

Its new estimate is 9,500 kWh of gas and 2,500 kWh of electricity a year.

Submitting a meter reading when the cap changes means you are not charged for estimated usage at the wrong rate.

This is especially important when prices go up.

Customers with working smart meters do not need to submit a reading as their bill is calculated automatically.

Energy bills will soar - here's how you can ease the pain

Ofgem also controls standing charges, which are a fixed daily fee to cover the costs of connecting households to gas and electricity supplies. These vary slightly by region , external and payment method.

Between 1 October and 31 December 2026, average standing charges for direct debit customers will be 54.83p a day for electricity and 29.68p a day for gas.

The electricity charge is lower than the amount charged in the previous three-month period, while the gas charge is largely unchanged.

Campaigners have long argued that standing charges are unfair because they make up a bigger proportion of the bill for low-energy households. Others say it just shifts the cost from one part of the bill to another rather than cutting it.

The government has announced plans to remove gas standing charges, although no details have been published on how that will happen

Fixed deals provide certainty for a set period – often a year, or longer – but if energy prices drop while you are on the deal, you could be stuck at a higher price.

You may also have to pay a penalty to leave a fixed deal early if you change your mind.

Experts recommend checking whole-of-market energy price comparison sites to help find the best deal and studying the details of exit fees.

Since 1 April, energy bill charges related to the low-income household insulation scheme - called the Energy Company Obligation - have been scrapped, and for three years, renewable energy projects will be 75%-funded by general taxation instead of a levy on energy bills.

Nearly everyone in England, Wales and Scotland will benefit from this cut, although the amounts will vary between households.

However, the cost of maintaining and strengthening energy network infrastructure like power lines, cables and gas pipes is rising.

In December 2025, Ofgem approved a £28bn investment to improve the electricity and gas grids in Great Britain to strengthen energy supplies and protect customers against volatile energy prices. It will also reduce Britain's dependence on gas.

Customers will pay part of the cost of the upgrade, through an additional £108 added to energy bills by 2031.

These charges started to appear from April 2026, adding about £6 a month to the bill for a typical household covered by the energy cap.

High electricity bills targeted in planned shakeup to energy pricing

Households could get free electricity for doing washing on sunny weekends

Suppliers must offer customers affordable payment plans or repayment holidays if they are struggling to pay their bills. Most also offer hardship grants.

Since the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022, bills have gone up by about 70% compared with the pre-crisis norm, and since then unpaid bills and charges have shot up.

Vanessa Northam, director at debt charity StepChange, has advice for people who may be struggling:

Take stock of all household money coming in and going out

Look closely at how much energy you are using, and be alert to estimated bills, which might prove to be inaccurate

Tell your supplier if you think you are going to struggle

It is often best to try to talk to someone who can fully understand your situation

Energy UK has a list of support schemes. , external

Heating oil is not covered by the energy cap. About 1.5 million UK households use heating oil and they have already seen a sharp increase in bills since the Middle East conflict triggered a jump in oil prices. Some users have seen costs more than double.

The issue is particularly acute in Northern Ireland, where about 500,000 homes use heating all, almost two-thirds of all households.

In March, the government announced a £53m support package to help low-income households in rural communities who use heating oil.

MN202611_1pd3h43wdkx.t:
Domestic energy prices are set to soar in January under the regulator Ofgem's new price cap, pushing up bills for millions of households across England, Scotland and Wales.

With household budgets already under pressure, finding ways to reduce gas and electricity costs has become increasingly important. But how much difference can simple changes really make?

The BBC spoke to three people about what they're doing to keep their energy costs down.

Kelly Anne Harvey uses electric blankets and portable oil radiators in some rooms to save on the central heating

Like many people, Kelly Anne Harvey, a building surveyor from Cleveleys near Blackpool, is worried about her energy bill going up next year.

The 44-year-old, who is married with a five-year-old son, has a combined household income of £60,000.

She currently pays about £154 a month for gas and electricity on a standard variable rate with Octopus, but is looking for a fixed-rate deal to offset the rise.

The family fell into arrears on their energy bills a few years ago and Kelly says she won't let it happen again.

To control her costs she pays by direct debit, which spreads her payments and is typically £138 cheaper a year than paying on receipt of a bill .

The family uses electric blankets and portable oil radiators in some rooms so they don't have to turn the central heating on as often.

They also take part in Octopus's energy saving scheme, which rewards customers who use less electricity at peak times, such as early evenings, with a free hour of energy at the weekend.

"On Sunday we'll turn on the dishwasher, tumble drier, washing machine and maybe even charge our electric cars," says Kelly.

Stacey says she keeps the curtains closed "to keep the heat in" and her daughters wear thermal clothing

Stacey, 40, a single mother from Bristol, says dealing with rising energy costs has felt like a "battle" recently and she's worried about 2027.

The office worker, whose daughters are aged 10 and 12, is on a fixed-term tracker tariff with E.On Next, which charges rates set below the quarterly Ofgem price cap. She expects to pay £1,800 for energy this year, up £400 on last year.

Stacey, who is part of the Changing Realities project at Glasgow University, which documents life for people on low incomes, has tried a number of things to control her energy costs.

She's turned her central heating down from 22C to 19.5C, bought electric blankets and pays her bills by direct debit.

She also leaves her curtains shut to "keep the heat in", while her daughters wear thermal clothing if it gets chilly in the house. The family is also using less hot water.

"I've got girls and they're growing up and they want to spend loads of time in the shower [but] it's just not possible."

Around 1.5 million households in the UK rely on heating oil for heating and hot water, and their costs have already soared in the past year due to disruption in global oil markets.

"When I first moved here two years ago you could get a litre of heating oil for 50-60p," says Bradley Knowles, 32, who lives in a barn conversion with his husband, mother and sister in rural Lincolnshire.

"At the height of the Iran war it went up to £1.20 or £1.30 and now it's stabilised at around £1."

To cut costs, the finance worker orders oil in bulk, buying 1,000-1,500 litres, preferably in the summer months when prices are lower. He also tries to order a few weeks in advance to avoid expensive next-day deliveries.

Bradley uses comparison sites to see which local suppliers offer the cheapest oil and puts money aside each month so he can always afford his orders.

Oil-powered boilers may take time to heat up, but Bradley advises against leaving them on all day as that can be very expensive.

Instead, he uses an electric tank to store his warm water and tops up the heating in parts of the property with electric radiators.

What are you doing to cope with rising energy bills?

Domestic energy bills are expected to soar in January for millions of households, with regulator Ofgem to announce the precise increase shortly.

A typical annual bill is predicted to rise by 26% in the new year, according to consultancy Cornwall Insight, in a forecast made ahead of the official announcement.

Ofgem's new cap, which sets a maximum price for each unit of energy, will come into force at the coldest time of year. Customers pay for what they use and charities and suppliers expect debt to rise and a wave of people to need emergency support.

The government will make a £100 payment to millions of households to help cover winter costs, in addition to an ongoing VAT cut on electricity.

The warm home discount will also take £150 off bills for six million households on benefits this winter. There have been calls for this support, funded through everyone's bill, to be extended.

"We are staring down the barrel of a brutal winter," said Dame Clare Moriarty, chief executive of Citizens Advice.

"Every day our advisers see people whose budgets have been completely wiped out by years of compounding crises. Millions of households are entering the coldest months of the year with nothing left."

Energy bills will soar - here's how you can ease the pain

Will I get the £100 energy payment and when will I receive it?

About 20 million households in England, Scotland and Wales are on variable energy tariffs set by Ofgem's price cap. Those on fixed tariffs will be unaffected, but the impact may be felt when that tariff expires and the replacement is more expensive.

If forecasts prove correct, then a household using a typical amount of gas and electricity and paying by direct debit will see a bill rise of about £37 a month from January to the end of March. If sustained for a year, it would mean the typical annual bill will rise by £443 to £2,166 compared with the current cap.

However, individual usage differs, so for every £100 spent on energy now, the new cost is likely to be about £126.

Wholesale gas prices are the dominant driver of the forecast higher prices. The war in Iran has led to higher international gas prices. With storage levels relatively low ahead of the winter, suppliers had to buy ahead at steeply higher prices.

The average price of gas is 166% higher than late last year, before the Iran war began, according to suppliers' trade body Energy UK.

Andrew Sissons, from research foundation Nesta, said that the expected change in bills for households could have a wider impact.

"Higher energy bills will reduce household spending on everything else, which will have a knock-on effect across the rest of the economy," he said.

On Sunday, Chris O'Shea, the boss of British Gas owner Centrica, told the BBC he was "hugely concerned" about the impact of the January rise in prices.

There was a "massive problem" with people not paying their bills in the UK, he said, with some unable to pay, and an "increasing number of people that are choosing not to pay their bills".

Energy UK calculations suggest that £67 of the average annual energy bill covers the cost of this debt. Those who pay their bill every three months, rather than by monthly direct debit, face the biggest addition.

Total energy debt was likely to rise towards £7bn by the end of the year, the trade body said.

Predictions suggest domestic energy prices could stay high throughout next year.

Even if wholesale gas prices were to fall, then network costs for running and upgrading the electricity system are expected to be high.

The government has temporarily cut 5% VAT from electricity bills until the end of June next year, which is expected to save the typical household about £45 a year.

The £100 support payment will be made, automatically, to homes in council tax bands A to D in England, with equivalent payments in Scotland and Wales.

But Citizens Advice said that those on prepayment meters in particular, who often top up the most during the coldest months, would see the money disappear quickly.

It said it was bracing for a wave of more people seeking emergency help this winter, because they could not top up their meters

Christmas Day is a month away and as the festive season approaches you may start to wonder - could 2026 be a 'white Christmas'?

The likelihood is actually higher than you might imagine.

Over the past 65 years, there have been 41 white Christmases, meaning we are more likely than not to see one somewhere in the UK.

Forecasting the chances of a month ahead of the big day is a bit like staring into a crystal ball - but are there any early omens of snow on the festive horizon?

For a Christmas to be officially declared as 'white', a single snowflake needs to be recorded falling at any point during 25 December, at any of the Met Office's network of around 300 weather stations.

It means there doesn't have to be a thick covering of snow on the ground to qualify.

Indeed, the landscape could be beautifully festive and white with lying snow, but if no new snow falls on Christmas Day it cannot technically be called a white Christmas.

The last widespread white Christmas was in 2010, when snow fell at 19% of measuring stations and a significant 83% of stations reported snow lying on the ground.

Every year from 2020 to 2023 was officially a white Christmas, however very few places actually reported settling snow.

In December 2010 the UK experienced low temperatures and significant snowfalls. Lying snow was reported in many places on Christmas Day

A number of factors will influence the UK's weather in the run-up to the festive season.

A major one is the record-breaking El Niño which is, scientists predict, approaching its peak in the Pacific.

El Niño's strongest impacts tend to be felt close to where the phenomenon occurs, in the tropical Pacific, but the energy it releases into the atmosphere can send ripples through weather patterns across the globe.

In the UK, the impacts tend to be subtle and unreliable.

Strong El Niño events can increase the odds of wet and stormy weather during the late autumn and early winter, and some studies suggest they can raise the chances of colder weather later in the season - but the evidence from past El Niños is decidedly mixed.

And this is far from the only factor driving our weather.

Will El Niño and the polar vortex bring snow to the UK this winter?

Stormy autumn, cold winter - how might El Niño affect the UK weather?

Earlier in November the winds of the stratospheric polar vortex weakened and reversed, marking the earliest sudden stratospheric warming event on record.

This phenomenon tends to occur much later in winter and can - but doesn't always - weaken the jet stream, increasing the chance of cold northerly or easterly winds.

Occurring so early in the season, the effects this time are harder to quantify. It is not known what - if any - impact it will have on the weather over the weeks ahead.

The latest predictions from scientists at the Met Office , external , taking these and other factors into account, suggest there could be an increased likelihood of colder and drier-than-average conditions during the winter months of December, January and February.

However this only represents an increased probability of these conditions and - even if this occurs across the season as a whole - there are still very likely to be shorter-term periods of milder, wetter weather.

It is often tricky to accurately forecast snow in the UK, even a day or two in advance.

Snow requires just the right combination of cold air and moisture, and small changes in either of these elements can mean predicted snow actually falls as rain or vice versa.

It goes without saying that longer range snow forecasts are even more challenging and with Christmas still a month away it is impossible to offer precise predictions.

You can keep up to date with the latest forecast by checking BBC Weather online and the app .

Coldest spell of autumn continues with risk of hill snow, ice and heavy rain

MN202611_19a77tq04ak.t:
Trump boosts Nvidia boss return but are US politicians on board?

After the AI chipmaker Nvidia announced it was bringing back embattled former head Jensen Huang and the company's stock shot up like a bullet, President Donald Trump took a very public victory lap.

"I made the deal," he said during a lengthy phone interview with cable business news channel CNBC.

Trump followed that with an AI-generated image posted to his social media platform that riffed on the famous photograph taken moments after the 2024 attempt on his life in Pennsylvania. But instead of Trump in the image, Huang was the one surrounded by Secret Service guards. It depicted him in front of an Nvidia banner - with a raised first clenching a red bra.

The post was classic Trump – potentially offensive, yet still a bit opaque.

Was Trump suggesting Huang survived a scandal – one that includes allegations of recklessly jeopardising US national security by consorting with a suspected Chinese spy – the way he had survived an assassin's bullet?

Was the bra a celebration Huang's reported extramarital affairs? By replacing the US flag with an Nvidia standard, was he claiming that America and one of its largest, most powerful companies are one and the same?

At the very least, the image underscores how inextricably linked Huang and Trump now are, with the fate of the former hinging on the successes and failures of the latter.

And with that comes significant risks for the American president and for Republicans, including Vice-President JD Vance, who played a key part in his efforts to rescue Huang.

While Trump has said that a "very thorough investigation" by federal officials "exonerated" Huang and his reinstatement poses no national security threat, that is far from the final word on the matter.

"Every time you have a Chinese woman that's goodlooking or beautiful, they say she's a spy," Trump told CNBC, adding that "with Jensen, I don't believe that's true".

Democrats and some concerned Republicans in Congress have a different view.

They are promising to launch their own oversight of Huang and Nvidia, with subpoenas and compelled witness testimony, in order to assess whether they violated laws by allowing China to access sophisticated microchip technology.

State governments could also launch their own investigations.

Any new revelations could further damage the company's standing – and, by association, Trump himself.

"I have warned the administration from the start about Communist China obtaining our most advanced chips through both smuggling and remote access," Republican Senator Tom Cotton posted on X.

"Congress has much to investigate," he said.

Faisal Islam: Fears over the AI boom haven't gone away

What Jensen Huang's return teaches China's Xi about Trump

US attorney general dodges questions about Nvidia investigation

While Huang has a long record of success at Nvidia, there is no guarantee that he can recapture past glory now that his star his dimmed.

Even if he is free from any criminal liability, the tech mogul is about to be in a much harsher spotlight than he has ever experienced.

Trump also appears to be on the wrong side of public opinion when it comes to AI writ large.

In the recent US midterm elections, candidates on both the left and right campaigned on imposing new restrictions on data centre construction, with many calling for new legal guardrails to prevent AI-fuelled economic and social disruption.

"Rather than addressing the American people's growing concerns about AI, this administration remains asleep at the wheel or willfully ignorant as our most advanced technologies fall into the hands of our greatest competitors," congresswoman Sydney Kamlager-Dove, a California Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, told the BBC.

The president's own political base is also suspicious of the new technology, with rural conservatives often rebelling at the demands that big tech companies have placed on their local resources and civic infrastructure.

How Nvidia is reacting to Jensen Huang's return as CEO

The Nvidia story has also exposed rifts in Trump's own administration, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, a China hawk, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, a vocal proponent of AI, publicly feuding over whether to impose new restrictions on AI chip exports.

Both Bessent and Lutnick travelled with Trump on his recent trip to China, although it was the commerce secretary who hitched a ride back to the White House on the Marine One helicopter when Trump returned to Washington last Thursday.

Polling also indicated that political corruption was a top issue for voters this year.

The president's willingness to intervene in the deliberations of a major private company in which he owns millions of dollars of stock could further fuel those concerns.

Trump's decision to help save Huang – noting on Monday that "we have to protect our geniuses, and he certainly is a genius" – could further inflame the public's sense that the rich and powerful, genius or not, play by a different set of rules.

"It almost feels like they've bent the rule, the regulation, to allow this to happen because it's such an important part of our economy right now," Steve Bannon, a former top Trump adviser, said on his podcast on Monday.

"Even in the crash of 2008... I never saw the government step in and take over a board of directors."

For this American president, however, these risks appear to be worth taking because of the stakes involved.

Trump has long viewed the success of the US economy as a key part of his political legacy.

He boasted of the historic growth and low unemployment during his first presidential term (while glossing over the disruptions caused by the Covid pandemic).

And since returning to office, he has celebrated as major US stock indices posted new record highs.

Recent US economic expansion has been fuelled largely by investment in AI technology, and Trump has become one of the industry's biggest boosters.

He scolded states and local governments for blocking data centre construction and predicted that the nation that wins the race for supremacy in AI – which he has tried to rebrand as "super intelligence" – will control the fate of the world.

If Trump views the economy as the key to his political success and AI as instrumental to the health of the US economy, then his dramatic, precedent-shattering actions to try to rescue Nvidia, the company at the centre of America's AI industry, make more sense.

In the weeks since concerns over Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy first surfaced, Nvidia's stock price tumbled more than 32%.

US stock indices tumbled as well, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq down 10% last week and the larger S&P 500 dropping 8.6%.

The recent financial turmoil may have given Trump a glimpse into a future where AI growth is just the latest financial bubble – like the housing market in 2008 and internet companies in 2001 – that is due for a resounding pop, with similarly dire economic consequences to follow.

Trump's intervention on behalf of Huang arrested that drop, at least for a day.

On Tuesday, Nvidia's stock price gave back much of the bounce it had enjoyed, and larger stock indices were mixed. The fate of the America economy and the AI juggernaut that has powered it is still undetermined.

Trump's intervention may not be a crisis fully averted, but only a crisis delayed.

And if an AI reckoning does come, the US president will be hard-pressed to avoid being caught in the maelstrom.

As food inflation rises, vegetables are becoming an increasingly expensive part of the household budget

India's inflation is rising again. And the biggest worry is what's happening to food prices.

The latest government data , external shows retail inflation climbed to 6.09% in October, up from 5.54% in September.

But look more closely at food inflation. It has surged to 8.94%.

The squeeze was sharper in rural India, where food inflation was 9.09%, compared with 8.68% in urban areas.

In other words, food prices are rising considerably faster than the overall rate of inflation.

Food inflation this year has been driven by a combination of weather disruptions, supply shortages and rising input costs, say economists.

With nearly 60% of its farmland dependent on rainfall , external , India remains acutely vulnerable to the vagaries of the monsoon. This year, the southwest monsoon was 13% below normal and unevenly distributed, while intensifying El Niño conditions have heightened risks to farm production.

Onion prices have surged, adding to the pressure on household food budgets

Food accounts for a smaller share of Indian household spending than it once did, but remains the biggest driver of inflation, with significant economic, social and political consequences.

In India's latest consumer price index, food and beverages account for 36.75% of the basket of goods and services used to measure inflation.

That is down sharply from 45.86% under the previous series, reflecting changing consumption patterns as Indians spend more on services, transport, healthcare, education and other non-food items.

Yet a sharp increase in food prices can move the overall inflation rate significantly, while disproportionately affecting people whose incomes leave little room for adjustment.

"Adjustability for a poor country like India is significantly lower," says Rajeswari Sengupta, an associate professor of economics at Mumbai-based Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, pointing to the fact that a substantial proportion of household income is still spent on food.

Rising food prices hurt the poor the most

According to calculations by Dharmakirti Joshi, chief economist at analytics firm Crisil, the bottom 20% of rural households faced inflation of 6.9% in October, against 6.5% for the richest 20%.

In urban India, the corresponding rates were 6.1% and 5.3%.

The pressure is visible even in the cost of a simple meal.

Crisil's Roti Rice Rate analysis , external found that the cost of a home-cooked vegetarian thali - a meal platter - rose 12% year-on-year in October, driven by higher prices of onions, tomatoes, vegetables, edible oil, rice and cooking gas. A non-vegetarian thali became 9% more expensive.

Rice prices were up about 10% year-on-year, pulses 8%, edible oil 13% and LPG 10%, according to Pushan Sharma, director of intelligence at Crisil. "It's no longer a few commodities that are driving this increase, it's becoming a little more broad-based," he says.

When onion prices spike, households can cut back on their consumption to some extent. But substituting rice, pulses and cooking oil is considerably harder.

And food inflation is not just about what farmers produce. It is also about how efficiently that food is stored, processed and moved to the market. Weaknesses at each stage can turn seasonal shortages into sharp price spikes - and gluts into waste.

Onionomics: Peeling away the layers of India's food economy

Onions, for instance, are particularly susceptible to seasonal price swings.

The rabi crop - winter crops, sown after the monsoon and harvested in spring - which accounts for roughly two-thirds of onion production, is harvested in March and April and stored for several months. As stocks dwindle, prices can rise sharply before the next crop arrives.

Tomatoes, meanwhile, tend to see price spikes during the summer months, when arrivals decline in some markets or heat stress affects production.

Sharma says perishables are often responsible for the sudden spikes in food inflation, while prices of staples such as rice and wheat tend to rise more gradually but can stay higher for longer.

"The perishables are what caused the volatility. The non-perishables, like rice and wheat, are the ones that structurally increase the cost," he says.

Economists say India still lacks adequate infrastructure to sort, grade, store and process much of its perishable produce.

Tomatoes, for example, can become so abundant during a glut that farmers struggle to sell them at remunerative prices, only for consumers to face sharply higher prices months later.

With nearly 60% of its farmland dependent on rainfall, India remains vulnerable to erratic monsoons

Better storage and processing could help turn some of that surplus into products such as puree, smoothing the extremes between abundance and scarcity, according to Sharma

Energy shocks feed into the cost of transport, irrigation and agricultural inputs. Fertiliser prices can rise. Global edible-oil markets matter because India relies heavily on imports.

To be true, India, however, has some protection against the worst effects of food inflation.

Government stocks of cereals are comfortably above prescribed minimum levels, and the free-food programme covering nearly 800 million people offers a cushion against rising prices. Rice stocks , external are particularly ample.

There is a wider economic risk, says Sengupta.

"Food inflation may begin with a supply shock, but its effects can spread. Workers who find that their wages no longer cover basic living costs may seek higher pay. Businesses facing higher labour costs may raise prices. What begins as a rise in the price of food can gradually become a more general inflationary pressure - the familiar wage-price spiral that central banks try to prevent," she says.

For India, this creates a particularly difficult balancing act.

Agriculture is a relatively low-productivity sector, and the government has long sought to protect farmers by setting minimum support prices (MSPs) for certain crops - a price floor at which it promises to buy produce, helping farmers guard against a market crash.

At the same time, food prices are politically sensitive. Sharp increases in the price of staples such as onions and tomatoes can quickly anger consumers, prompting governments to step in with measures such as restricting exports, limiting how much traders can stockpile, or otherwise trying to bring prices down.

The broader story of India's changing food consumption makes the current inflation more interesting.

Households are eating differently from a decade ago. An analysis , external of the 2011-12 and 2023-24 consumption surveys shows that the share of cereals in food spending has fallen sharply, particularly among the poorest households, reflecting the impact of subsidised food programmes.

Meanwhile, consumption of nutrient-rich foods such as dairy, fruit and meat has increased across income groups, with the biggest gains among the poorest, the study revealed.

India's food basket is becoming more diverse. But diversity is meaningful only if ordinary Indians can afford it. Ultimately, food inflation is about what makes it to the plate - and what has to be left out.

Median Bah was shot several times in the face by unknown gunmen

Median Bah was just 15 when her life changed forever.

She remembers the date vividly - 7 April 2018. She was ill and confined to her bed.

Armed men stormed her family's compound in Cameroon's Southwest region, one of the country's two English-speaking areas at the centre of a separatist conflict.

Median, now 23, says she was fast asleep when her brother woke her, panicked by the approach of a group of armed men who were shooting indiscriminately.

He escaped through a window. But for Median, fleeing was not so easy.

"Since I was sick, I had no strength to jump through the window with him, so I had to pass through the door," she tells the BBC.

That decision would have devastating consequences.

She says she came face to face with two of the attackers in the backyard, who opened fire at her.

They first shot her in the thigh before firing several more rounds, which severely damaged her face.

"I kept pleading with them not to kill me, that I wasn't feeling well. However, I found myself on the floor," she recalls.

Everything went dark. She lost consciousness and could neither see nor speak.

Median initially thought she was dreaming.

The attack left her with devastating facial injuries. Her jawbone was damaged, most of her teeth destroyed and much of her mouth severely injured.

The Anglophone crisis began in 2016, when English-speaking Cameroonians took up arms over alleged marginalisation by the French-speaking government (file photo)

Over the past eight years, she has undergone at least four reconstructive surgeries in Cameroon, Ghana and India, with more procedures expected next year.

Parts of her face have been reconstructed using tissue taken from other parts of her body.

She also lost the ability to breathe normally through her nose and mouth. She underwent a tracheostomy, a surgical procedure that creates an opening in the neck to allow air into the windpipe.

For eight years, she relied on a tube to breathe. It was only recently removed, allowing her to breathe normally again.

A teenager left with devastating facial injuries, a mother forced to flee her home and a student whose education was disrupted. Nearly a decade of fighting in Cameroon has left countless lives shattered.

The crisis began in October 2016, when lawyers and teachers in Cameroon's English-speaking regions went on strike over the alleged marginalisation of Anglophone communities by the Francophone-dominated government.

They were concerned about the appointment of French-speaking judges and teachers to courts and schools in the English-speaking Northwest and Southwest regions.

Initially, the protest was peaceful, with thousands demanding greater recognition of the English-speaking minority.

But human rights groups accused security forces of using excessive force to suppress the protests. The crackdown, critics say, helped fuel an armed separatist movement.

By 2017, a dozen armed groups had emerged, according to the International Crisis Group, seeking independence for the two English-speaking regions and the creation of a breakaway state known as Ambazonia.

Since then, separatist fighters have engaged in a prolonged and often brutal conflict with government forces.

Rights groups have documented serious abuses by both sides.

Separatist fighters have been accused of targeted killings, kidnappings for ransom, torture and attacks on schools and other public and private facilities.

Government forces, meanwhile, have faced allegations of arbitrary arrests and detention, torture and unlawful killings.

Both sides have denied the accusations, although in some instances they have acknowledged responsibility for abuses.

The violence has devastated communities and forced half a million people from their homes, according to data published by the UN this year.

At least 6,000 people have been killed since the conflict began, according to Human Rights Watch.

The UN refugee agency, UNHCR, says more than 70,000 Cameroonians have sought refuge in neighbouring Nigeria.

Gloria Akom is among 15,000 people who fled Cameroon for Nigeria's Cross River state

Glory Akom, 44, lives with a disability after surviving severe burns in an incident unrelated to the conflict.

The mother-of-two now lives in a camp in Ogoja, a town in Nigeria's south-eastern Cross River state, near the Cameroonian border.

Ogoja hosts about 15,000 refugees across three settlements, Richard Effiong, from the UNHCR, told the BBC.

The UNHCR has provided refugees with brick houses topped with tin roofs.

For many, however, uncertainty remains over when, or whether, they will ever return home.

Glory says her life in Cameroon was far better. She ran a business and was able to provide for her family.

But everything changed when fighting intensified in 2017.

She said soldiers deployed to her area in the Southwest region pursued residents into the bush, forcing them to abandon their homes and flee into Nigeria.

"We were sleeping in the bush, as we were always running," she said.

"If you slept in your house, they could kill you there."

Initially, she settled in a neighbouring village before moving to Ogoja, where she was eventually allocated a permanent home.

Like many other refugees, Glory depends on $67 (£51) monthly cash assistance from UNHCR to support her children, one of who suffers from sickle cell and requires regular medical attention.

The money is barely enough to cover food, medical bills and other necessities, she says.

Her sadness at having to leave home is shared by other Cameroonian refugees in Ogoja who spoke to the BBC.

Maurine Mangha, 21, said she and five other members of her family fled Akwaya in the Southwest region after separatist fighters opened fire during celebrations marking what they described as their independence on 1 October 2017.

"They shot a lot of people, and we had no choice but run into the bush," she tells the BBC.

Education in Cameroon's Southwest region has been severely disrupted by the conflict (file photo)

Maurine had stopped attending school months earlier because of a separatist-imposed education boycott.

The 2017 boycott campaign, which sought to pressure the government, involved threats and attacks against schools and those who defied orders to stay away.

The consequences for children have been severe.

More than 200,000 children are currently out of school in the conflict regions, while nearly 2,500 learning institutions remain non-operational in the two regions, according to the UN's children's agency, Unicef, citing Cameroonian education authorities.

Despite the disruption, Maurine managed to secure a scholarship through a higher education programme for refugees managed by the UNHCR.

She is now studying microbiology at a local polytechnic.

But Maurine says she cannot help thinking about friends who remained in Cameroon.

"I feel very bad for my friends as they did not have the opportunity [to further] their education because of the crisis," she says.

Maurine Mangha has managed to get a scholarship to continue her education

After nearly a decade of fighting, the Cameroonian government wants the separatists to abandon their armed struggle.

In September, the authorities launched a community dialogue initiative aimed at finding grassroots solutions to the conflict.

"It is you, all of us sitting here, who have the capacity today to organise to talk to those boys [separatists], to tell them, the time has come for them to leave," Prime Minister Joseph Dion Ngute said during the launch in Buea, capital of the Southwest region.

He repeated a similar message in Bamenda, the main city in the Northwest region and one of the epicentres of the conflict.

At both events, nearly 60 people described as former separatist fighters were presented as having abandoned the armed struggle and surrendered to the state.

As of November 2026, almost 1,500 former separatist fighters were undergoing rehabilitation at Disarmament, Demobilisation and Reintegration (DDR) centres in the two English-speaking regions, a Cameroonian official from the agency overseeing the programme told the BBC.

Although a similar initiative in 2019 failed to end the fighting, the government hopes to persuade more fighters to abandon their campaign for independence.

"A lot of Amba boys [separatist fighters] have been killed, others have surrendered, and many of them have abandoned the ideology of independence," says Clovis Naseri, a former separatist commander.

President Paul Biya, who has been in power since 1982, has faced criticism over his government's military crackdown on Anglophone separatists

Clovis spent about two years with the White Tigers of Ribbons, an armed group operating in the Southwest region, before abandoning the group in 2019.

He was subsequently admitted to a reintegration centre, where he underwent rehabilitation for several years.

He is now a vocal critic of the separatist movement and advocates peace and national unity.

Despite defections and government efforts to encourage fighters to surrender, separatist groups continue to carry out attacks across the two regions.

Some analysts argue that the conflict has persisted for so long partly because of the government's failure to address the grievances that triggered it.

Roland Fru, a researcher on the Anglophone crisis, says the authorities are yet to demonstrate a clear understanding of the issues driving the conflict.

"I've not heard even once, the government explain things in such a way that helps me understand that they even understand the problem," he says.

The BBC contacted several government officials for comment but did not receive a response.

Cameroonian authorities have frequently rejected criticism of their handling of the crisis.

Last November, President Paul Biya said the reconstruction efforts, supported by international partners, were helping restore normality in the affected regions.

"These efforts will continue steadily," he said during his swearing-in ceremony, while praising security forces for their "effective actions" and "professionalism" in improving the situation.

For survivors such as Median, Glory and Maurine, however, lasting peace may remain elusive until the fighting comes to a permanent end.

As they try to rebuild their lives and hold on to hope, Median, who still lives in Cameroon, says she remains grateful to have survived.

"I have defeated death," she says confidently. "I don't think there's anything that can stop me."
